lessons.title: Abattoir buildings and services
lessons.html:
Infrastructure that supports hygiene

The regulations under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 set structural requirements for abattoirs, and the provincial veterinary services approve plans before building or major changes. A foreman must understand why the infrastructure is designed as it is, so it is used and maintained correctly.

Layout principles

  • Forward flow: product moves in one direction, from live animal to dispatch, without crossing back.
  • Separation: dirty areas (lairage, stunning, hide, gut room) are physically separate from clean areas (dressed carcass, chillers, deboning, dispatch).
  • Separate entrances for workers in clean and dirty areas, with change rooms, boot washes and hand wash points.
  • Separate routes for edible product, inedible material, hides and waste.

Surfaces and finishes

Floors must be impervious, non-slip and sloped to drains. Walls must be smooth, light-coloured and washable to a suitable height. Junctions between floors and walls are coved (rounded) so dirt cannot collect. Ceilings must not drip or flake. Doors and frames must be of non-corroding material.

Services

ServiceWhy it matters
Potable waterAll water touching meat and equipment must be fit to drink; it is tested regularly
Hot waterFor sterilisers, hand washing and cleaning
LightingAdequate intensity at inspection points; protected fittings
VentilationRemoves steam and heat; prevents condensation
RefrigerationChillers, freezers, cooled deboning rooms
Effluent treatmentRemoves blood, fat and solids before water leaves the site, in line with the National Water Act 36 of 1998 and municipal by-laws
Standby powerKeeps refrigeration running during load shedding and outages

lessons.title: Equipment and technology on the line
lessons.html:
Key equipment

  • Restraining and stunning boxes: hold the animal still for accurate stunning, reducing stress and failed stuns.
  • Overhead rails and powered chains: move carcasses through the stations at a controlled speed.
  • Hoists and spreaders: lift carcasses safely.
  • Hide pullers: remove cattle hides mechanically, reducing contamination and labour if correctly operated.
  • Carcass splitting saws: split carcasses accurately; sterilised between carcasses.
  • Synchronised offal conveyors or trays: keep offal next to its carcass for inspection.
  • Scald tanks, dehairers and singers for pigs.
  • Knife and equipment sterilisers at every station.
  • Carcass washes: manual or automatic cabinets.
  • Scales, labelling and data systems: record mass, classification and owner.

Technology and data

Modern abattoirs use electronic systems to link each carcass to its owner, lot, mass, classification and inspection result. Barcodes or RFID tags on hooks or carcasses allow automatic tracking. Chiller temperatures are logged electronically with alarms. Data from these systems can show yield, throughput and condemnation trends per supplier.

Automation

Automation replaces manual tasks with machines, for example automatic splitting saws, brisket cutters, robotic carcass washing and automated vision grading in some countries. Benefits include consistency, higher throughput and fewer repetitive strain injuries. Costs include capital investment, maintenance skills, dependence on electricity and spare parts, and the need to retrain or redeploy workers. In South Africa, where labour is relatively available and many abattoirs are small, automation is often focused on the steps where it most improves hygiene, safety or consistency.

lessons.title: Maintenance and safe use of equipment
lessons.html:
Keeping infrastructure working

Damaged infrastructure creates hygiene and safety risks: cracked floors hold dirt and water, broken wall panels hide pests, rusty rails drip onto carcasses, failing seals let warm air into chillers.

Maintenance types

  • Preventive maintenance: planned servicing at set intervals, such as lubricating chains with food-grade lubricant, replacing saw blades and checking refrigeration.
  • Condition monitoring: regular checks to find wear before failure, for example vibration or noise from motors, or chiller temperatures drifting up.
  • Breakdown maintenance: repairs after failure. Aim to keep this to a minimum.

Hygiene during maintenance

Maintenance staff must follow the same hygiene rules as production workers in clean areas. Tools are cleaned before use near meat. After repairs, the area and equipment are cleaned and inspected before production restarts. Only food-grade lubricants may be used where they can contact meat.

Machine safety

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 requires machinery to be safe and operators to be trained.

  • Guards must always be in place on saws, hide pullers and conveyors.
  • Use lock-out and tag-out before cleaning or repairing machines: isolate the power, lock the isolator, attach a tag and test that the machine cannot start.
  • Only trained and authorised people may operate or repair machines.
  • Emergency stop buttons must be visible, reachable and tested.
  • Report damaged cables, leaks and unusual noises immediately.

Key points

  • Abattoir layout follows forward flow and separates clean and dirty areas.
  • Surfaces must be impervious, washable and coved at junctions.
  • Services include potable water, hot water, lighting, ventilation, refrigeration, effluent treatment and standby power.
  • Automation improves consistency but needs investment, skills and reliable power.
  • Use lock-out and tag-out and keep guards in place.
